title: Science close

cards: For ninety days this path has lived in the lab. Meditators and scientists at one table. A gorilla people missed.
A habit curve that forgives a missed day. A stranger on crutches in a waiting room, seminary students in a hurry, a nerve with too many promises hung on it.
Then a long, uncomfortable stretch on studies that didn't hold up. Today the lab door closes, and the question is simple: what do you carry out, and how tightly do you hold it?

teach.b: First, the four rooms: attention, then habit, then compassion, then the honest part: replication, placebo, sleep, money, purpose and the edge of what can be measured. Second, two piles.

Some findings held up well across studies and are worth building on: attention is limited, habits take shape slowly and survive a missed day, slow breathing can settle the body, kindness can be practiced.

teach.h: WHAT HELD UP, AND WHAT STAYED SHAKY.
teach.b: Other claims stayed shaky: single studies never repeated, popular stories that ran ahead of their data, big promises about one nerve or one hormone. The skill wasn't memorizing the piles.
It was learning to ask, each time, how big is the claim, and how strong is the evidence? Third, two old voices asking the same.

In the Buddhist Kalama Sutta, the Buddha tells the Kalamas, townspeople confused by rival teachers, not to accept something just because of tradition, report or a teacher's authority, but to take it up when they know for themselves it leads to good.

teach.h: KNOW FOR YOURSELVES; PROVE ALL THINGS.
teach.b: And Paul writes to the church at Thessalonica, in the King James Bible: "Prove all things; hold fast that which is good." Different traditions, a shared habit: test, then hold. Fourth, the shape of it.
Hold the solid things firmly enough to practice them every day; hold the rest lightly, open to being wrong. Tomorrow the path leaves the lab for the world's schools of practice, starting with Zen.

how: People who draw on both science and tradition often keep practices with solid evidence as daily habits, while holding newer or single-study claims loosely until they're tested again.

o: the end of ninety days in the lab: test, then hold
the claim that science has closed the case on faith
a lab rule that every study must be repeated twice

s: the block's goal was to memorize which findings are true
the skill was asking, each time, how big the claim is and how strong the evidence.
Paul writes: prove all things; hold fast that which is good
in 1 Thessalonians, in the King James Bible.
holding a claim lightly means throwing it away
it means keeping it open, ready to be wrong, while you hold the solid things firmly.

games.q: a new single study goes viral: a practice rewires your brain in a week. after ninety days of honest science, what do you do?
o: decide all science is hype and ignore it.
try the practice if it helps, and hold the claim lightly until it's tested again.
games.why: that's the habit of this block, and an old one: "prove all things; hold fast that which is good."

practice: Open both hands on your knees, palms up. In the right, place one thing from these ninety days you're keeping for good; in the left, one claim you're no longer sure of, not thrown away, just resting there, open.
Breathe between the two, and if you pray, you can offer both hands as they are.

wordCard.voice: Science close. Ninety days through attention, habit, compassion and the honest part, and one habit to keep: test, then hold. A week and a block end here. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: solid and light. Firm enough to practice, loose enough to learn. Ninety days, done.

sources.q: Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
